front: Three critical research areas of biotechnology
back: (i) Providing the best catalyst in the form of an improved organism, usually a microbe or pure enzyme. (ii) Creating optimal conditions through engineering for the catalyst to act. (iii) Downstream processing technologies to purify the protein/organic compound.
Therapeutics, diagnostics, genetically modified crops for agriculture, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment and energy production.
Any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube, under sterile conditions in special nutrient media.
The capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant. Established by scientists during the 1950s.
The method of producing thousands of plants through tissue culture, in very short durations. All the plants are genetically identical to the original plant.
Each plant produced by micro-propagation — genetically identical to the original plant from which it was grown.
A carbon source such as sucrose; inorganic salts; vitamins; amino acids; and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins. The culture must be sterile.

Isolated naked protoplasts of two different plant varieties, each with a desirable character, are fused to give a hybrid protoplast that is grown into a new plant. The hybrid is a somatic hybrid; the process is somatic hybridisation.
The somatic hybrid formed by fusing a tomato protoplast with a potato protoplast. It was achieved, but did not have all the desired combination of characteristics for commercial utilisation.
Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation.

front: Five benefits of genetic modification in crops
back: More tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat); reduced reliance on chemical pesticides; reduced post-harvest losses; increased efficiency of mineral usage; enhanced nutritional value, e.g. golden rice — Vitamin 'A' enriched rice.

An insecticidal protein produced by the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, which forms protein crystals containing it during a particular phase of growth. The gene has been cloned and expressed in plants to create a bio-pesticide.

front: Why Bt toxin does not kill Bacillus thuringiensis
back: In the bacterium the toxin exists as an inactive protoxin. It is converted to the active form only in the alkaline pH of an insect gut, which solubilises the crystals.

front: Mode of action of Bt toxin in an insect
back: The insect ingests the inactive protoxin; the alkaline pH of the gut solubilises the crystals and activates the toxin; the activated toxin binds to midgut epithelial cells, creates pores, and causes cell swelling and lysis, eventually killing the insect.

Genes coding for Bt toxin proteins. cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms; cryIAb controls corn borer. The choice of gene depends on the crop and the targeted pest, as most Bt toxins are insect-group specific.
Lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).
A method of cellular defense occurring in all eukaryotic organisms: silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation of the mRNA.

front: Sources of the complementary RNA in RNAi
back: Infection by viruses having RNA genomes, or mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.

Nematode-specific genes are introduced using Agrobacterium vectors so the plant produces both sense and anti-sense RNA. These form dsRNA, which initiates RNAi and silences the specific mRNA of Meloidegyne incognitia, so the parasite cannot survive.

About 30 have been approved for human use the world over, and 12 of them are presently marketed in India. They do not induce unwanted immunological responses, as is common with products isolated from non-human sources.
Two short polypeptide chains, A and B, linked together by disulphide bridges. In mammals it is first made as a pro-hormone containing an extra stretch called the C peptide.
An extra stretch present in the insulin pro-hormone. It is not present in mature insulin — it is removed during maturation into insulin.

Two DNA sequences corresponding to chains A and B of human insulin were prepared and introduced into plasmids of E. coli. Chains A and B were produced separately, extracted, and combined by creating disulfide bonds to form human insulin.

A collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect that has been diagnosed in a child or embryo. Genes are inserted into a person's cells and tissues to treat a disease, and a normal gene is delivered to take over the function of, and compensate for, the non-functional gene.

Given in 1990 to a 4-year old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. ADA is crucial for the immune system to function, and the disorder is caused by deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase.

Lymphocytes from the patient's blood are grown in culture; a functional ADA cDNA is introduced using a retroviral vector; the cells are returned to the patient. Because the cells are not immortal, periodic infusion is needed. Introducing the ADA gene at early embryonic stages could be a permanent cure.

Recombinant DNA technology (probe hybridisation and autoradiography), PCR (amplification of the pathogen's nucleic acid) and ELISA (antigen-antibody interaction). Conventional serum and urine analysis cannot detect a disease early.

A single stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule, allowed to hybridise to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells and detected by autoradiography. A clone with a mutated gene gives no signal because the probe has no complementarity with it.

Enzyme Linked Immuno-sorbent Assay; based on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction. Infection is detected by the presence of antigens (proteins, glycoproteins, etc.) or by the antibodies synthesised against the pathogen.

Animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene. Rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, but over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

front: Five reasons for producing transgenic animals
back: Normal physiology and development (e.g. insulin-like growth factor); study of disease (models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer's); biological products (e.g. alpha-1-antitrypsin for emphysema); vaccine safety; chemical safety testing.
Produced human protein-enriched milk at 2.4 grams per litre. The milk contained human alpha-lactalbumin and was nutritionally a more balanced product for human babies than natural cow-milk.
Genetic Engineering Approval Committee, set up by the Indian Government. It makes decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM-organisms for public services.

An American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office, allowing it to sell a 'new' variety in the US and abroad. That variety was derived from Indian farmers' varieties — Indian Basmati crossed with semi-dwarf varieties — claimed as an invention or novelty. The patent extends to functional equivalents.

The term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned, and without compensatory payment.

front: Why the patent debate is unequal
back: Most industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge. The developing and underdeveloped world is rich in biodiversity and in traditional knowledge related to bio-resources, which can be exploited to develop modern applications and to save time, effort and expenditure in commercialisation.
Recently cleared by the Indian Parliament to address such issues, including patent terms, emergency provisions, and research and development initiatives.
